design_detail: A 'For Debate' article in Addiction (2008;103:1060-1062; three pages, 26 references) by six researchers at the Universities of Bristol and Bath, arguing for a 'translational' approach (animal experiments to test hypotheses raised by epidemiology, then corroboration in clinical and population studies) with one case study: whether alcohol raises the risk of a heroin or opiate overdose through a pharmacological interaction. It is an argument and a short review of selected evidence, not a systematic review: no search, selection criteria or appraisal is described. It quotes figures from other papers (listed in its reference list) that were not read for this card. Read in full from the PDF, including the declaration of interest and reference list.
can_establish: What six researchers argued, in 2007 to 2008, the existing evidence on alcohol and opioid overdose death showed and did not show; which other explanations they thought fit the same evidence; and what kind of study they thought was needed.
cannot_establish: How strongly alcohol raises the risk of opioid overdose in people (no new data, no pooled estimate, no figure for risk); that the figures it quotes (alcohol in about half of heroin-related deaths, about a third of methadone-related deaths; 60% lower blood morphine when blood alcohol was above 100 mg/dl) are complete or accurate, because the underlying studies were not read; or that the evidence it describes is all the evidence there was.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (opinion and review article; no search described). Evidence quoted comes from post-mortem and audit studies of heroin and methadone deaths in the UK, Sweden, the United States and Australia, a hair-analysis study, and reviews.
sample.selection_effects: The studies quoted were chosen by the authors to support a case for further research; the article does not say how many other studies exist or whether any found no relation between alcohol and opioid levels at post mortem. Post-mortem samples include only people who died, so they cannot show how often alcohol was present in people who used opioids and did not die.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Alcohol and opioid exposure is described as measured in the cited post-mortem studies (blood alcohol and blood morphine concentrations).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; a figure quoted from cited studies (blood alcohol above or below 100 mg/dl) is a post-mortem measurement, not a dose.
exposure.polysubstance: The article states that heroin or methadone were detected as sole agents in only a small proportion of deaths, with no figure; alcohol is described as the most common other substance detected.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The post-mortem studies it quotes compared dead people with high and low blood alcohol; no living comparison group is described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The article names the main alternatives itself: alcohol might impair judgement of tolerance and safe use; alcohol use is linked to heroin relapse; people who have stopped or reduced heroin may drink more, so low or falling tolerance could be the underlying problem; and polydrug use may mark people at higher risk for other reasons.

outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the article does not mention post-mortem redistribution of drugs or other limits of post-mortem concentrations that the review by White and Irvine (1999) raises.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures quoted from other papers: alcohol detected in about 50% of heroin-related deaths and about a third of methadone-related deaths (four cited sources); a significant inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem in multiple studies of heroin deaths (four cited); morphine blood concentrations 60% lower in heroin-related deaths with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl than below it in studies in the United States and Australia (two cited); opioid levels at autopsy often below the predicted fatal range for highly tolerant people (one hair-analysis study).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative article.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An argued summary of post-mortem and audit data: opioid overdose deaths rarely involve a single drug; alcohol is the most common other substance; blood morphine tends to be lower when blood alcohol is higher; and morphine levels at autopsy are often below those expected in highly tolerant people. The authors say this pattern is consistent with a pharmacological interaction and is also consistent with lost or low tolerance, relapse, impaired judgement and shared risk factors, and that they cannot be told apart without experimental evidence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that people who drink may need less heroin to overdose, 'all other factors being equal', because of a pharmacological interaction; the text says the interaction 'remains unproven', that the effect of alcohol and heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated systematically, and that animal experiments should test it. These claims are measured and the article states its own alternatives. One statement goes beyond its source: that overdose risk appears to rise after incarceration or detoxification, which it cites to White and Irvine (1999), who describe only a period of abstinence.

timeline.event: Ruttenber, Kalter and Santinga (J Forensic Sci): the role of ethanol in heroin-related death (as quoted by this article; not read)
Levine, Green and Smialek (J Forensic Sci), with Darke (1999): lower blood morphine with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl in heroin-related deaths (as quoted by this article; not read)
White and Irvine review the pharmacology of breathing depression and of loss of tolerance; the source this article cites for risk after a break in use

Lintzeris and colleagues, diazepam given with methadone or buprenorphine under high-dose conditions: named by this article as an example of a clinical challenge study of breathing (as quoted; not read)

replication.where_it_stands: A position paper and secondary source. Its post-mortem facts trace to four to six earlier studies not read here; its main contribution is to state the evidence limits (an inverse blood alcohol and morphine pattern and frequent co-detection fit several explanations) and to call for experimental tests. It is a source for what was and was not established by 2008, not for the size of any effect.

funding.funder: No grants were involved in the writing (Declaration of interest, p. 1062).
funding.declared_conflicts: Several co-authors receive funding from the pharmaceutical industry for some of their research (Nutt, Lingford-Hughes, Henderson); no other agencies requested the paper (p. 1062).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Social Medicine, Community Psychiatry and Pharmacology at the University of Bristol, and Pharmacology at the University of Bath. One of the 26 references (reference 6, a London audit of overdose deaths) has the first author as first author. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Animal experiments of opioid and alcohol effects on breathing at realistic blood levels, linked human clinical challenge studies of breathing with and without alcohol, and epidemiological studies that test whether drinking tracks with reduced opioid use or relapse; and, as the article says, a controlled trial is unlikely to be feasible.

domains.note: No methods; the quoted studies were chosen by the authors to make a case.

It explains why observational associations can mislead and lists alternative explanations for the post-mortem pattern; it does not appraise the specific post-mortem studies it quotes or mention post-mortem redistribution of drugs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 26 references (a London audit of overdose deaths) is by the first author; it is cited for toxicology findings alongside other sources.
Consistently worded as 'consistent with', 'may' and 'remains unproven'; hypotheses and evidence are kept apart.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the main conclusions
domains.note: It sets out alternatives to the interaction hypothesis well, but cites only studies that found an inverse relation or frequent co-detection of alcohol, and does not say whether any studies found otherwise.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative article (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The article is careful about what its evidence does not show, but it has no search method, quotes figures from papers not read here, and is an argument for a research approach. It may be cited for what the authors said was and was not established in 2008, for its list of alternative explanations, and for the facts it quotes with their sources, flagged as second-hand. It may not be cited for the size of any alcohol effect on opioid overdose risk, for the safety or danger of any level of drinking, or for a statement about incarceration or detoxification, which it attributes to White and Irvine and they do not make.

key_findings.finding: The abstract argues for a translational approach using one case study. It says the positive epidemiological evidence is that opiate overdose deaths rarely involve a single drug, that alcohol is the most common other drug involved, that blood alcohol and morphine concentrations at post mortem are inversely related, and that post-mortem morphine levels are often below those expected for highly tolerant people. It says this is consistent with the hypothesis of a pharmacological interaction but does not rule out other causal and non-causal pathways, such as alcohol being linked with lower tolerance or being confounded by other factors; experimental evidence is needed, unlikely to come from further epidemiology or randomised trials.

Overdose is described as the main cause of excess mortality linked with injection opiate use in the UK and many other countries; risk 'appears to be increased' after periods of relative abstinence, for example after incarceration or detoxification, 'probably because tolerance is decreased' (cited to White and Irvine, 1999). Many reviews suggest that concomitant use of other depressant drugs, particularly alcohol, raises the risk of fatal opiate overdose.
key_findings.note: White and Irvine mention a period of abstinence and naltrexone treatment only; they do not mention incarceration or detoxification.

key_findings.finding: Toxicology shows substantial polydrug use, with heroin or methadone detected alone in only a small proportion of deaths. Alcohol is the most commonly detected substance in heroin-related deaths (about 50%) and in approximately a third of methadone-related deaths (cited to four sources); multiple studies of heroin deaths report a significant inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem; studies in the United States and Australia found blood morphine 60% lower with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl than below it; autopsy opioid levels in people with a history of dependent heroin use were often below the predicted fatal range for highly tolerant people; alcohol levels at post mortem were not particularly high.

The prevailing interpretation is that alcohol and opiates have additive or interactive effects on breathing so that less heroin is needed for a fatal overdose. The authors list other routes: alcohol may impair judgement of tolerance and safe levels; alcohol use is associated with heroin relapse; people who have stopped or are reducing heroin may drink more, so low or falling tolerance could be the underlying problem; and polydrug use may mark people at risk for other reasons. They say the issue of causality matters because it changes how to intervene.

Observational epidemiology and case series have a history of producing associations later found misleading, even when repeated across studies and backed by a plausible mechanism (hormone replacement therapy and heart disease given as an example); observational evidence generates hypotheses but is poorly placed to test them; a controlled trial of alcohol and fatal overdose risk would be challenging and raises practical and ethical issues.

Euphoric and breathing-depressant effects of morphine and heroin both come from mu-opioid receptor activation, and tolerance to breathing depression has been seen in animals and humans; studies of whether alcohol in turn affects mu-receptor function are 'extremely limited'; the effect of alcohol with heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking 'has not been evaluated systematically' and a pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic interaction 'remains unproven'.

Proposal: animal experiments to test whether alcohol changes opioid effects on breathing, translated to human relevance through linked clinical challenge studies (one example cited is diazepam given with methadone or buprenorphine) and epidemiological studies of whether drinking tracks with reduced heroin use or relapse; animal evidence alone, even if replicated, would be insufficient to direct public health action.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 5th paragraph (end of p. 1061) and 7th paragraph (pp. 1061–1062)

key_findings.finding: A prevention message aimed at drinking around opioid use would differ from one aimed at loss of tolerance and relapse; the authors say which applies matters for how alcohol use is managed in people who use opioids.

A further unanswered question named: to what extent and for how long opiate substitution drugs confer tolerance to the breathing depression of heroin, i.e., how long patients are protected if they relapse or take heroin on top of a prescription.
Declaration of interest: several co-authors receive funding from the pharmaceutical industry for some of their research; no grants were involved in the writing of the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that overdose risk appears to rise after incarceration or detoxification is cited to White and Irvine (1999), but that review describes only 'a period of abstinence' and naltrexone treatment; it does not mention prison release or detoxification.
reporting_issues.consequence: The specific settings are the present authors' addition; cite White and Irvine only for the general idea of lost tolerance.

reporting_issues.issue: The figures for alcohol in heroin-related deaths (about 50%), methadone-related deaths (about a third), the inverse relation with blood morphine and the 60% lower morphine level are given without sample sizes or years, as reference numbers only (the 60% figure names only the United States and Australia).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures can be used only as quoted, with the sources listed; the studies were not read here.

reporting_issues.issue: Post-mortem blood concentrations are used as evidence of dose and interaction without mentioning that they may not reflect the situation at the time of death (post-mortem redistribution, time to sampling, site), a limit that White and Irvine (1999) state.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inverse blood alcohol and morphine relation may be partly a post-mortem artefact as well as a tolerance or interaction effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the epidemiological evidence is 'consistent with the hypothesis' of an interaction 'all other factors being equal', while the text says the effect on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated; the 'all other factors being equal' condition is not one that post-mortem data can show.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read the abstract's sentence as a statement about consistency, not as support for an effect; whether other factors were equal cannot be told from post-mortem data.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1060-1062 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Hickman_2008_AlcoholOverdoseDeathTranslational.pdf), full text including abstract, declaration of interest and reference list. The cited primary studies were not read.
